about: Truso (Janow Pomorski on Lake Druzno), the amber market of the Este, 793 to its end about 1000 and the reeds after. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/truso.md, the spine (silver_road, cast.wulfstan), peoples/baltic_east.md and the chain amber_road, whose people (Ketil, Gedune, Drua, Nameda, Wigmar) are given their faces here. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified; local flags begin tr_. ports_793.json closes Truso in 850: the dossier and the audit say about 1000, and this file is written for 1000. Cards here should read ch_amber_road_truso_shut, changed_ests_bar_strangers and changed_ests_brew_ale.

ports.summary: Truso is a market of craftsmen and traders on the reedy shore of a shallow lake behind the Estmere, in the land of the Este, seven days and nights east of Sliesthorp. No king's penny counts here and no toll is known: amber, honey, wax, furs and people are weighed against cut silver on folding scales. A merchant comes for amber at the source, and stays because the Este's customs are worth more to know than their prices.
ports.seasons: Ice shuts the lake and the lagoon from about Martinmas to Easter (?). The amber is gathered after the autumn and winter gales and is cheapest when the first boats come in spring; the honey comes in after Lammas; by autumn the sheds are bare and the fast horses are being fed up for the winter's burnings.

history.text: A letter of King Theodoric of the Goths, kept in a collection made about this year, thanks the Aesti of this shore for a gift of amber and explains to them what amber is. The king had died in 526.
history.source: Cassiodorus, Variae V.2, as cited in en.wikipedia 'Old Prussians' (dossier 7); the date of the letter itself is before 526 (?)

history.text: About now, by one reckoning, the market on the lake begins; by another, not until late in the next century.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Truso' and the Elblag museum (end of the 7th century); pl.wikipedia 'Truso' (late 8th century); dossier 1

history.text: A working market, busiest in the sailing months and not yet at its largest. No event is recorded.
history.source: dossier 5; the picture for 793 is the dossier's safe reading of the disagreeing dates

history.text: In this year or soon after, a purse of eleven whole coins and five pieces is put in the ground at Truso: ten dirhams of the caliphs and one drachm of the Persian king Khosrow, two hundred years old. Nobody comes back for it.
history.source: Medievalists.net, 28 Sept 2026 (the deposit dug in 1986; youngest coin 814/815)

history.text: In the first half of this century dirhams reach the country round: six more and two pieces lie in woodland to the north.
history.source: Medievalists.net, 28 Sept 2026 (the Mlynary coins, studied by Dr Jakub Jagodzinski)

history.text: About now, by one account, the traders settle the year round with their families and build long houses.

Wulfstan sails from the Heaths to Truso in seven days and nights, the ship running under sail all the way, and afterwards tells King Alfred of the Este: their kings, their mead, their cold and the riding for a dead man's goods.
history.source: The Old English Orosius (texts_793.json wulfstan, Bosworth 1859; the customs from Sweet 1883, pp. 19-21); the year is about 880 (en.wikipedia 'Wulfstan of Hedeby') or about 890 (en.wikipedia 'Truso')

history.text: The latest amber and antler work that can be dated is of about these years.
By one account works of defence are raised about now.
In the second half of this century the silt of the Nogat begins to cut the lake off from the lagoon and the sea, and a new harbour at the Vistula's mouth takes the trade.

Bishop Adalbert of Prague comes by sea to the Vistula's mouth after Easter, enters the country of the Bruzi on 17 April and is killed some days after the 22nd, somewhere in this land; a priest of idols named Sicco is said to have struck first. Duke Boleslaw buys the body for its weight in gold. No Life names Truso.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Adalbert of Prague'; the Lives of Canaparius and Bruno, not read (?)

history.text: In this century or about this year the place burns: a thick layer of ash, burnt timbers and many arrowheads. Who did it is not known. The people scatter into the country round.
history.source: en. and de.wikipedia 'Truso'; en.wikipedia 'Elblag'. The year is not known (?)

eras.text: A summer market growing into a town. Danes and Gutes keep houses on marked plots along the shore, the Este hold the fort on the rise and the country behind, and the first silver with the Saracens' writing is a thing men pass from hand to hand and bite. Amber is cheap in spring and nobody asks whose man you are.

The silver comes steadily now, whole and cut, up the Vistula and across from Gotland. More houses, more scales, more men who bury a purse under a post before they go inland. The comb-makers and amber-cutters work with their doors open from the thaw to the first ice.

The traders winter here with their wives and children; long houses of three rooms stand where booths stood (?). Children on the shore speak Danish to their fathers and the Este's tongue to everyone else. Grobin is gone quiet and its Gutes have come here or gone home.

The town at its fullest: twenty hectares of plots, workshops and boats. An Englishman from the Heaths walks about asking why the dead do not rot, and writes nothing down because he cannot write; he remembers it instead, in order.

Still busy, but the silver is of a new kind and comes by other roads, and the best amber goes north to Kaup on the Sambian shore (?). Fewer new houses. The old craftsmen's sons take a share in a ship and do not come back to the bench.

A ditch and a bank where there was open ground (?). Each spring the channel through the reeds is narrower, and skippers who used to come up to the houses now lie in the Ilfing and send a boat. A new harbour at the Vistula's mouth takes the ships. Men carry bows to the shore.

Ash under the grass, charred posts, a few fishers' huts. Reeds stand where the boats lay. The Este of the country round still gather amber and still burn their dead; they sell at the Vistula's mouth now, and nobody under forty has heard the name Truso said as a place one goes to.

sites.name: The boat shore
sites.see: A low shore of grey shingle and trodden reed with boats drawn up side by side, their sterns in brown still water. Behind them the plots and thatched houses, and behind those a rise with a timber fort and smoke. In front, women kneel at cloths spread with wet yellow lumps. Frogs, a caulking mallet, the smell of tar, lake mud and smoked bream.
sites.source: Boat wreckage and ship rivets on the shore (pl.wikipedia 'Truso', digs of 1985-86); Lake Druzno shallow and reed-ringed (en.wikipedia 'Lake Druzno'). A dug harbour basin is reported by the excavator (?). The sellers on cloths are the game's (chain amber_road)

sites.name: The mouth of the Ilfing
sites.see: Where the river leaves the lake: a gap in the reeds marked by nothing at all, fish traps of withy on either side, three log boats with men standing in them. Northward the water widens to the pale Estmere and a line of sand beyond it. Herons, the slap of a net, the smell of mud and fish scale. The fishers look at every boat and say nothing.
sites.source: Wulfstan: the Ilfing comes into the Estmere 'out of the lake on whose shore Truso stands', and there is 'very much fishing' (Old English Orosius). The fishers who count boats are the chain's (amber_road s05). Where the lagoon opened to the sea is not known (?)

sites.name: The weighing ground
sites.see: A trodden space between the shore and the first plots, with no stalls: men stand in pairs, one holding a little folding scale up to the light, the other watching the pans. On the ground, sacks of amber, tubs of honey, wax in cakes, marten skins tied in forties, and a row of people sitting with their ankles roped. The talk is quiet. Silver clicks on bronze.
sites.source: Scales, weights and cut dirhams from the dig (en. and sv.wikipedia 'Truso'; Medievalists.net 2026); amber, furs and slaves (en.wikipedia 'Elblag'); honey (Wulfstan). No market place has been identified as such, and no toll or law is known (dossier 2, 4): there is no toll site in this file on purpose

sites.name: The Dane's long house
sites.see: A post-built house of three rooms on a marked plot, twenty paces long, its thatch nearly to the ground. Inside, a long hearth, benches with strangers' sea chests under them, a gaming board on a barrel, a scale case hanging from a peg. Smoke, wet wool, mead. Through the end door the lake shows grey between two boats.
sites.source: Three-room post-built houses of 50 to 120 square metres on regular plots (pl.wikipedia 'Truso'; about 6 by 21 m, en.wikipedia 'Truso'); gaming pieces and boards (sv.wikipedia (?)). That one house took guests is the game's (chain amber_road). The drink is mead: no ale is brewed among the Este (Wulfstan)

sites.name: The amber-cutters' row
sites.see: Small houses with their doors propped open to the south for the light. On each threshold a board, a knife, a bow-drill and a heap of honey-coloured chips; finished beads hang in strings from the door post and turn in the wind. Raw lumps soak in a bowl of brine to show which float. It smells of warm resin, like a pine wood in the sun.
sites.source: Amber-working at Truso, dated late 8th to early 10th century (pl.wikipedia 'Truso'; en.wikipedia 'Lake Druzno'). The tests (rub, brine, lip) are the chain's and are true of amber

sites.name: The comb-makers and the glass fire
sites.see: A plot heaped with antler: tines in one pile, sawn plates in another, a drift of white dust underfoot. A man rivets tooth-plates between two bars; next door a woman winds a thread of green glass round an iron rod over a clay hearth, and a bead grows on it. The rasp of a saw, the hiss of the bellows, burnt horn.
sites.source: Antler-working (combs above all) and glass-working at Truso (pl.wikipedia 'Truso'). The craftsmen are not named in any source

sites.name: The smith and the goldsmith
sites.see: Two hearths under one roof at the edge of the plots, away from the thatch. At one a smith draws out rivets by the handful; at the other a small man with a blowpipe bends over a crucible no bigger than an egg. On a plank between them lie brooches, weights of lead and bronze, a sword without its hilt. Charcoal smoke and the ring of the hammer.
sites.source: Smithing and goldsmithing, weights, swords and Scandinavian jewellery from the dig (pl. and en.wikipedia 'Truso'). 'change_coin' here means silver cast or cut to a weight: there is no mint and no coin of the place (dossier 4)

sites.name: The menders' strand
sites.see: The north end of the shore, where a boat lies on her side with three strakes off. Barrels of tar stand in the shade, a keg of new rivets beside them, moss drying on a hurdle. Two men split an oak log with wedges and do not hurry. Beyond them, in the reeds, the black ribs of a boat nobody mended.
sites.source: Boat wreckage and Scandinavian ship rivets (pl.wikipedia 'Truso'); riveted boats of 9 to 11 m by 2.5 to 3 m, tar barrels and unused rivets (Design/content/ships.md, from an abstract (?))

sites.name: The fort on the rise
sites.see: Higher ground behind the town, palings of split oak, a gate with a horse skull over it. Inside, log houses close together and one larger than the rest, its door shut and a store beside it with a bar across. Men sit on the bank with bowls of mares' milk. From the gate the whole lake lies below, and a straight road runs inland over the rise.
sites.source: Wulfstan: the Este have many strongholds, 'and in each stronghold there is a king'; the king and the richest men drink mares' milk. He does not say Truso had a king, and no fort has been dug here: this one is the game's and the chain's (?). Whether the traders' shore had an Este lord over it is not known (dossier 8). If flag changed_ests_bar_strangers is set, a stranger is not seated here; if ch_amber_road_truso_shut, the player's house is not let through the gate

sites.name: The mile road
sites.see: A straight track from the fort gate over open grass to a rise about a mile off, worn hollow by hooves. On most days there is nothing on it but a boy leading a lean horse at a walk, and another, and another: more horses than a place this size should feed. On one day in a season there are heaps of goods along it and the whole country at the palings.
sites.source: Wulfstan: a dead man's goods are laid in five or six heaps, the largest about a mile from the town, and ridden for from five or six miles off; 'fast horses are very dear there' (Old English Orosius, Sweet 1883; our rendering). The horses sold here are goods_793.json horses

sites.name: The burning ground by the river
sites.see: A strip of blackened turf between the houses and the Ilfing, with low mounds along the bank, some old and green, some raw. Women go over a cold pyre with wooden rakes, slowly, looking for bone. A pot stands ready. Nobody speaks loudly. The wind brings the smell of wet ash and, from the mounds, nothing.
sites.source: Wulfstan: every man, of whatever people, must be burnt, and if one bone is found unburnt a great atonement is owed. 'Merchant graves along the river' (en.wikipedia 'Truso'); a large cemetery dug in the 1920s (de.wikipedia 'Truso'). No 'bury' here: nobody may lie unburnt in this ground

sites.name: The wood nobody cuts
sites.see: South of the houses the alders stand in black water, old and uncut, though the town burns wood all year and fetches it from farther off. A path of laid branches goes in a little way and stops at a spring. Rags of cloth hang there, and a bowl. Fish rise in the pools and no trap is set. It is cool, and quieter than it should be.
sites.source: Woods, fields and waters so holy that none cut, tilled or fished there, and Christians kept from the groves: Adam of Bremen IV.18, of the 1070s, so later than most of the game and placed here by the game (?). No temple or idol is known at Truso. No high priest and no 'Romove': those are of 1326 (dossier 6)

people.name: Ketil
people.trait: A Dane who has kept a house and a pair of scales on this shore for half his life: he weighs for both sides and never says what is in the pan.
people.want: To know how the cold is made. Failing that, a skipper who comes back each spring and tells him what the west is saying.
people.fear: A guest dying under his roof with a bone left whole; and outliving his usefulness to the fort.
people.voice: Slow, amused, exact. Explains the Este as a man explains his wife's kin: fondly, and with his voice down.
people.looks: About forty-five in 793, broad, grey in a plaited beard, a blue cloak pinned at the shoulder, folding scales in a round bronze case at his belt and a bag of weights that clinks when he sits.
knows: what amber, honey, wax and marten fetch here this moon, and what they fetched at Sliesthorp when the last ship left
which bowl to take in the fort, and where a stranger may sit
the law of the pyre and what an unburnt bone costs
every kind of silver that has crossed his pan, and which of it is base
who is in from Gotland, from Birka and from the Wends

ties.note: keeps his house by the fort's leave and turns the king's words into Norse
twelve winters asking how the cold is made; twelve winters not told
weighs her heaps and keeps his mouth shut about them, which is the whole of their bargain
the boy's father died in his house; he let the son stay
his son's daughter, born after his death; she has his scales
the Svea lodges with him on the way to the Vistula and checks his weights against Ketil's, every time
buys captives from the fort's wars on Asulf's silver and ships them to the Heaths
the Wend sells wax and honey four days nearer the west
his sister is married to old Botgair's son, among the Gotlanders on the Curonian shore; the two men have traded amber prices through her for years (?)
the Curonian go-between's son sends him false amber prices by every ship; he sends false ones back, and both know the true
a goldsmith on the Danes' river in Skane whose weights came off the same mould as his; they tried them against each other once, and each pretends to doubt the other's
the fisherman who brings his guests through the reeds; Ketil pays him in salt and has never been told how many boats the fort hears of

lines.greet: A Frisian boat, and small. You came the whole way in that? Then you can count, or you are lucky. Sit. I will find out which.
lines.greet_again: The same boat. I told the fort a Frisian would be back with the open water. They said strangers do not come twice. Mead?
rumour: Do not look for one king to complain to. Every fort in this land has its own, and no two of them are friends.
A Svea came through with silver that had writing like worm tracks on it. Good silver. I cut one in half to be sure, and he did not blink.
The Wends keep their fast horses at home now. They have learned what a fast horse is worth here on a burning day.
A man from the fort asked me what a penny is. I said: silver a king has spoken to. He asked if it weighs more afterwards.
lines.on_pennies: Your king's head is very fine. Put it in the pan. Here the king's head weighs what the king's head weighs.
lines.saying: I weigh. I do not say what is in the pan. That is how a Dane keeps a house on this beach.
lines.farewell: Seven days if the wind is kind, the Wends' land on your left hand going home. Tell them at the Heaths that Ketil still weighs true.

people.source: Invented: the chain amber_road's host, and the spine's 'Danish craftsmen with scales' (silver_road hook for Truso). Scandinavians are plain in the finds and are credited with founding the place (en. and pl.wikipedia 'Truso'). Name: Ketil, common on Danish rune stones. His son Toli keeps the house from 824 to about 846 and is not written here

people.name: Gedune
people.trait: The dead king's brother and then king of the fort: a horseman who has never been in a boat and judges men by what they do with a bowl.
people.want: The fastest horse in Witland, and to be owed by strangers rather than to owe them.
people.fear: The fort up the Ilfing, whose king is his cousin; and a burning of his own so poor that the riders go home early.
people.voice: Speaks through the Dane. Short questions, long silences; says a thing once and has it said twice in Norse.
people.looks: About thirty-five in 793, lean, long fair hair, clean chin and a heavy moustache, a neck ring of twisted bronze, a belted wool tunic, riding whip in his hand even on foot.
knows: which forts are at war this summer and which road is shut for it
what is in the king's store and when it will be opened
horses: every fast one between the Vistula and the sea, and whose it is
what atonement the law asks, and from whom

ties.note: his tongue toward the sea, tolerated and useful
his mother's sister; her kin kept his brother cold
she sells on the beach what should come up to his store
took the boy's father's atonement, or burned him well: either way there is a reckoning
the man who speaks for the Cori of the coast to the north, whose boats raid his amber shore; Kantegede answers that he speaks for traders (?)
the Wends beyond the Vistula sell the horses he wants and keep the best
the fisherman who brings the fort its fish and the count of boats that came through the reeds; Gedune trusts the count, and has never asked about the faces

lines.greet: You came by water. My brother said men who come by water leave by water. Drink, and we will see what you are first.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. You drank what you were given and you came back. Sit higher this time.
rumour: My cousin up the river has a grey horse. He says it is for his own burning. He should be careful what he wishes for.
The barley is for horses. The honey is for slaves. The milk is for men. I am told you do all this differently and are still alive.
There is fighting on the Sambian road. Nothing will come down it before the hay. Buy what is here.
lines.on_strangers: A stranger may ride for the heaps. A stranger may win. Then he is not a stranger, and has things to lose here.
lines.saying: A slow horse eats as much as a fast one.
lines.farewell: Go. Bring cloth. Bring a horse if your boat will hold one and you are not afraid of it.

people.source: Invented: the chain amber_road's heir. A king in each stronghold, much fighting among them, mares' milk for the king and the richest, fast horses dear (Wulfstan, Old English Orosius). The name is built in the manner of Old Prussian names recorded centuries later (?); no person of Truso is named in any source

people.name: Drua
people.trait: An old woman of the kin that can make cold: sent for when a great man dies, feared a little, and bored by being asked how.
people.want: A girl of her own blood with the patience to learn it. Her daughters married horsemen.
people.fear: That it ends with her; and warm winters, when the lake ice is thin and grey.
people.voice: Few words, in her own tongue. Looks at a person for as long as it takes to count them.
people.looks: Past sixty, small and upright, a grey wool shawl over her head pinned with a bronze spiral, hands red and cracked from cold water, a covered clay pot always within reach.
knows: how long each dead man in the fort has lain and when he will burn
half of how the cold is made, which she may show, and half she will not
which woods and waters may not be touched
weather: what kind of winter is coming, from the alders and the geese

ties.note: her sister's son; she remembers him afraid of horses
the Dane always wants to know how
taught her as a girl to tell true stone from boiled resin by the lip
his mother's mothers were of her kin; five lifetimes on they still cut the lake ice at midwinter
the woman who is asked on the Cori's shore; they send each other dried roots by the amber boats and have never met
her brother's son, who takes ships through the reeds and cuts the lake ice for her kin at midwinter

lines.greet: Another one from the water. Stand there. Do not touch him, and do not ask.
lines.greet_again: You did not ask last time. Good. Ask this time and I may be in a mood.
rumour: The geese went early. Cut your ice thick this winter, or do not die in summer.
A man of the west died in the Dane's house. He wanted to lie in earth. Earth here does not want him.
The alders by the spring are budding on the north side first. Somebody cut a branch. It was not one of ours.
lines.on_cold: Two bowls, one of water and one of your barley drink. Come at first light and tell me which is harder.
lines.saying: Fire is quick and everyone can do it.
lines.farewell: Go home warm. It is all your people know how to be.

people.source: Invented: the chain amber_road's cold-wife. Wulfstan: one kin among the Este can make cold, so that the dead lie long and do not rot; set down two vessels of ale or water and they freeze one over, summer or winter (Old English Orosius, Sweet 1883; our rendering). How is not known; winter ice kept in a pit is the modern guess (?)

people.name: Santirme
people.trait: A fisherman of the Ilfing who brings strangers' ships across the Estmere and up the river to the houses: the pilot of the lake in the Dane's day, and the first of a line that keeps the pole.
people.want: Salt, iron hooks, and a skipper who does what he is told the first time.
people.fear: The reeds. They stand a little further out each spring, and nobody but his kin is counting.
people.voice: A few Norse words, all of them orders, and a great deal said with the pole. Laughs without sound.
people.looks: A lean brown man with a shaved chin and a long moustache, bare legs, an eelskin belt, a sounding pole marked with rings of red wool.
knows: this spring's channel across the Estmere and up the Ilfing, and where last spring's was
every boat that came in since the thaw, and which sat low going out
where his father's sister's kin cut the lake ice at midwinter, and no more about it than a man is told
that the pilot on the Cori's bar is called the best on this sea by skippers who want his own fee lowered

ties.note: his father's sister; he cuts the lake ice for her kin at midwinter and does not ask where it goes
brings the Dane's guests through the reeds to his door and is paid in salt, by Ketil's own weights
brings the fort fish and the count of boats; of faces he says he has no memory
the pilot of the Cori's bar; each has heard the other called the best on this sea, from skippers who wanted a lower fee
the pole, the red wool and the marks come down in his line to a fisherman five lifetimes on, who takes the last ships through

lines.greet: You. Stop. Sail down. Pole here, in my hand. Now your man steers where I point, and nobody talks.
lines.greet_again: The same boat. Deeper than last year. Good trade, bad for me. Give the pole.
rumour: The reeds come out one boat's length in my lifetime. My father said the same. Nobody counts but us.
A Gotlander went up the big river with long iron, in a small boat. He sat low. He did not come down.
The man on the Cori's bar digs his river out with spades. Here the water is honest. Only shallow.
lines.saying: Deep water forgives. Shallow water remembers.
lines.farewell: East stake, then the open. Come lighter, or come earlier in the year.

people.source: Invented: the pilot of the Este's lake of grobin.tulegaud's tie, in the years to 826; truso.mante holds the same pole in the 900s. Wulfstan: the Ilfing runs out of the lake on whose shore Truso stands, into the Estmere (texts_793.json wulfstan); the silting that ends the harbour is of the later 900s (en. and pl.wikipedia 'Truso'), here only foreseen. The Gotlander with the blades is the story truso.eleven_and_five. The name is an Old Prussian personal name of later record (?)

people.name: Nameda
people.trait: A gatherer's widow who sells gleanings on a cloth at the shore: cheerful, sharp, and entirely willing to sell a stranger boiled resin at the price of sea-stone.
people.want: Frisian cloth for her daughters' cloaks, and a buyer clever enough to be worth cheating.
people.fear: The king's store taking the beach trade; and a spring with no gales behind it.
people.voice: Market Norse in pieces, said fast, with a laugh at the end. Teaches by letting you lose.
people.looks: About thirty, sunburnt, strong forearms, hair under a linen cloth, a row of bronze spirals sewn to her apron, wet sand to the knees and a forked amber rake over her shoulder.
knows: what the last gale threw up and on which shore
the three tests: the sleeve, the brine, the lip
who among the gatherers sells behind her back, and for how much
the words for everything on her cloth, and will teach them to a buyer who buys nothing

ties.note: he weighs and does not say; she knows he keeps to it
learned the lip test from her, and how to keep a straight face
what she sells on the shore never reaches his store
her daughter's daughter married into the Dane's house: Asfrid has her eye for a heap
has never met the bead-maker; knows his taste in stone from what the skippers refuse (chain amber_road)
cheated the Frisian once, taught him why, and has not managed it since
a Frisian who cuts beads at the Wends' market gets her stone through Wigmar's hands and pays a season behind; she gives him credit, a little

lines.greet: Sea-stone. West shore, after the storm. All good. You have honest eyes: I will take your silver gently.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian who rubs every piece on his sleeve. Sit. Today I have nothing false. Nearly nothing.
rumour: North gale three nights at the dark of the moon. We stood in the water to the waist with nets. The sheds are full; do not tell the Dane.
A Gute bought my whole middle heap by eye. I liked him very much. I hope he comes again.
Stone as big as a fist, with a fly in it, legs and all. The fort took it. A fly, and they call me a cheat.
lines.on_tests: Sleeve: it pulls chaff. Brine: it swims. Lip: it is warm. Glass is cold, resin stinks. Now you know, and I am poorer.
lines.saying: The sea gives it for nothing. The carrying up the beach is what you pay for.
lines.farewell: Come when the ice goes. First boat gets first heap, and I sort it less carefully when my hands are cold.

people.source: Invented: the chain amber_road's seller. Amber gathered after storms and sold in spring (Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 2.14 (?)); bronze spirals sewn on women's aprons are attested for Finnic graves, here borrowed for a Balt (?). The name is built in the manner of later Old Prussian names (?)

people.name: Wigmar
people.trait: A Frisian from the Weser mouth whose father died here: baptised, alone among heathens, and too stubborn to go home poor.
people.want: A partner from the west with a boat, so that cloth comes east and amber goes west without a Dane's hand on both.
people.fear: Dying here himself and being burned; he keeps a boat ready for it and has told the fishers why.
people.voice: Dry and quick, glad of his own tongue. Says the Our Father under his breath when he passes the burning ground.
people.looks: Seventeen in 795 and thin, later a spare weathered man with a short Frisian cloak, a little wooden cross on a thong inside his shirt, a notched tally stick in his belt.
knows: what Frisian cloth fetches in marten skins, to the skin
the way in: the gap in the spit, the Estmere, the Ilfing, the lake
which skippers at the Heaths are honest about what amber sold for
his father's riddle, about a thing that was water and will be water again

ties.note: house room, and the atonement Ketil risked for his father
pays the fort a cloak a year to be let alone
she cheated him once, taught him why, and has not managed it since
a Dorestad skipper who carried his father's last cargo west and paid the widow in full
in old age hears there is a priest at the Heaths and sails seven days to be shriven (after 850)
baptised as a child in Liudger's country; it is all the teaching he had
taught the child of the Dane's house to count in Frisian; she still prices amber in it when she does not want to be understood
a countryman at the Wends' market, whose raw amber he sends down the coast on trust, a season behind

lines.greet: You speak like the Rhine mouth. Say something else. Anything. I have not heard it since my father stopped talking.
lines.greet_again: The only other baptised skipper on the lake. Sit by me, so the Dane has two of us to laugh at.
rumour: They give a marten skin for a wool cloak here and think they have robbed you. Bring cloth. Bring all the cloth there is.
I asked the fishers what day Easter falls. They told me when the ice goes. It is nearer than my own guess most years.
A Svea at the Dane's house keeps an English boy who tallies for him. The boy crossed himself when he saw my cross, and then looked at his master.
lines.on_father: He wanted earth and the last day. Whatever you think of what was done, you were there, and nobody else from home was.
lines.saying: A short cloak dries quickest. The Franks laugh at it until it rains.
lines.farewell: Cut the stick with me before you go: your half, my half. Then one of us at least must come back.

people.source: Invented: the chain amber_road's son of Wigbod. Frisian goods at Truso (de.wikipedia 'Truso'); marten for woollen cloaks among the Prussians (Adam of Bremen IV.18, later). The short Frisian cloak: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34. The English boy is the spine's cast.tidwine with cast.holmfast (holy_island), passing through; the split tally is the felag of the chain's unlock_partner_wigmar

people.name: Asfrid
people.trait: Ketil's granddaughter, born here: an amber-cutter who keeps his scales and the house's memory of every skipper who ever lodged in it.
people.want: The fly in amber the fort took from her mother's mother; and steady buyers now the silver comes by other roads.
people.fear: The channel through the reeds, which is a little narrower each spring, though nobody else will say so.
people.voice: Danish at home, the Este's tongue in the street, and a third way of talking for strangers: slow and kind and missing nothing.
people.looks: A woman of middle years, fair hair under a cloth, two oval bronze brooches with a string of her own amber beads between them, a bow-drill in her lap, the old round scale case at her belt.
knows: the name of every house that lodged with her grandfather, and whether it paid
amber: the cut, the drill, what the Svear want and what goes to the Rus
which marks on a dirham are the caliphs' and which are older
where under the old house floor a guest's purse was left, and that he never came back

ties.note: her father's father; she never saw him and quotes him daily
her mother's mother's mother, by the beach side of the family
the old Frisian taught her to count in his tongue when she was a child
answers the English skipper's questions for three evenings and sells him a string of rough amber at the end, on a promise of English cloth
the Svea house has left weights in pledge with hers since her grandfather's day
a Gute who mends the house's boat each second summer and is paid in beads (?)

lines.greet: A Frisian house. Wait. My grandfather had a Frisian who came in a boat too small for the passage. Was that yours?
lines.greet_again: The house with the small boat. He said you would keep coming. He is fifty years dead and still right about people.
rumour: The new silver is thin and broad, from farther east than the old. It weighs the same. Everything weighs the same; that is the comfort of a scale.
A man from the Heaths is asking about the dead, an Englishman. Polite. He remembers things in rows, like beads on a string.
The Gutes at Grobin have all gone home or come here. Something went badly with the Cori. Nobody says what.
lines.on_purse: A guest put eleven coins and five pieces under our floor and went up the Vistula, in my grandfather's last summer. We do not dig under a guest's post.
lines.saying: My grandfather said: weigh, and do not say what is in the pan. I say what is in the pan. Times change.
lines.farewell: Go before the wind turns. And look at the reeds as you go out: tell me next year if I am imagining it.

people.source: Invented. Women with Scandinavian brooches, amber-working, scales (en. and pl.wikipedia 'Truso'); traders settled with families about 850 (sv.wikipedia (?)); Grobin's Scandinavians gone about 850 (peoples/baltic_east.md (?)). The purse is the deposit of 814/815 dug in 1986 (Medievalists.net 2026): that it was a guest's is the game's

people.name: Mante
people.trait: A fisherman of the Ilfing who takes ships through the reeds: the last man who knows the channel, and the first to say aloud that it is closing.
people.want: To get his sons' boats down to the new harbour at the Vistula's mouth before there is no water to float them.
people.fear: Bowmen in boats; and being the one left to explain to strangers where the town was.
people.voice: Rough Norse learned from skippers. Counts boats under his breath while he talks to you.
people.looks: A weathered man with a shaved chin and long grey moustache, bare legs, a sealskin cap, a sounding pole twice his height marked with rings of red wool.
knows: the channel: this spring's, not last spring's
every boat that came in or went out since the thaw
where his mothers' kin cut the lake ice, and what they do with it, as far as a man is told
who is selling up and going to the Vistula's mouth, and what they will take for a house

ties.note: of her kin through his mother, five lifetimes on
her grandchildren were the last on the shore to pay him in beads
the fort's king in his day is Gedune's line; Mante brings it fish and the count of boats
the first of his line known to have held the pole at the river mouth, in the Dane's day; the red wool and the marks came down with it

lines.greet: Stop there. You draw too much. Give me the pole and your steersman's ear, and do what I say when I say it.
lines.greet_again: The house with the ship's dog on the sail. Your grandfather came up to the houses under oars. You will go in on a rope.
rumour: A hand less water than at the last thaw. The river that feeds the Estmere is dropping its mud at our door.
They have built a harbour at the Vistula's mouth, with a wall. The Gutes go there now. It is nearer the sea by a day.
A shaved man with a book came among the forts after the thaw. They killed him. A duke paid his weight in gold for what was left.
lines.after_fire: It burned in one night. Arrows first, then fire. I was on the water. Do not ask me who: I counted boats, not faces.
lines.saying: Reeds are patient. They only have to stand there.
lines.farewell: Out by the east stake, then north until the spit shows. If you come again, come light.

people.source: Invented. The silting of the Nogat in the later 10th century, Gdansk taking the trade, the ash layer with many arrowheads, the people scattering (en., pl. and de.wikipedia 'Truso'; en.wikipedia 'Elblag'). Who burned it is not known and he does not say. The shaved man is Adalbert, April 997 (en.wikipedia 'Adalbert of Prague'): not at Truso. The name is in the manner of later Old Prussian names (?)

stories.title: The cold house and the mile
stories.summary: The king of the fort is dead and lies cold in his own house while his kin drink his goods away; the store with the amber is shut until he burns. On the day, what is left is laid in heaps along a mile of road and ridden for, strangers too.
stories.picture: A straight road running from a palisade gate over grass to a rise, heaps of amber, furs and silver along it, a dust of riders far off, and in front a Dane with scales and a Frisian skipper at the gatepost.

beats.text: A bead-maker sorts amber that has come through three hands and says where it comes from: seven days east of the Heaths, a river mouth and a lake.
Boats on the beach and nothing for sale. Ketil comes down with his scales; a steward holds out two bowls, milk and mead, and which you take is where you sit.
The dead king on his bench, ten weeks dead, the room as cold as the bottom of a well. Drua sits by two bowls skinned with ice.
Nameda's three heaps on a cloth: sea-stone, boiled resin and yellow glass, one price for all. Ketil weighs and looks at the lake.
Wigmar's father dies in the Dane's house, baptised, and the law says every man is burned. The son promised him earth.
The burning is named for the second new moon. Gedune wants a horse, or the barley drink and someone who can make it.
Two moons to find a fast horse or a brew-wife, or to come back with nothing but cloth.
The heaps are out along the mile and the whole country is at the palings.
On the Cori's shore the woman who is asked has a bundle of dried root for the kin who keep the cold at the lake of the Este. She has never met them. The amber boats carry it, and yours could.
Drua takes the bundle, smells it, and names the sender. She sends back the root that brings sleep. Of how the cold is made she says what she has said to the Dane for twelve winters.

endings.how: You sat out the wake and watched the riding from the gate.
endings.text: The store opens next morning and the amber is sold in three days. Ketil grows old with a boat to wait for. The Este go on exactly as they were.
endings.reward: Sixteen to twenty-six sacks of amber at the source price, and one of: Ketil as your factor, the way in, Wigmar as partner, a chest of cold (chain amber_road, E2).

endings.how: You carried a horse seven days in the boat and rode it.
endings.text: The horse is sung about and you are 'the Frisian who was on him'. Gedune gives his hand. Nothing in the custom changes.
endings.reward: The heap you reached; unlock_title_est_guest_friend, and the silvered bridle or ground by the lake (chain amber_road, E1).

endings.how: You poured ale at the wake, brought a brew-wife and served at the fire.
endings.text: A brewhouse stands inside the palings and barley has a price. Two lifetimes on, an Englishman is told that at one fort they brew.
endings.reward: Sets changed_ests_brew_ale; the work truso.work.brewhouse, or the king's peace on your boat (chain amber_road, E3).

endings.how: You robbed the near heaps while every eye was on the road.
endings.text: Ketil pays the atonement with his house and goes to Grobin. Strangers are held behind a line of stakes on the beach.
endings.reward: Silver, at Sliesthorp, and the fort shut to your house: ch_amber_road_truso_shut, changed_ests_bar_strangers unless you send amends (chain amber_road, E4).

stories.reward: The amber trade learned from the people who gather it, and a name in the fort: the chain amber_road carries the cards and the payouts.

stories.title: What the king's head weighs
stories.summary: At Dorestad the moneyer says silver must be struck; at Truso nobody has ever seen a penny taken at its face. Ketil puts the house's deniers in his pan beside a cut coin of the caliphs and an old king of Persia, and asks which the Frisian would rather be paid in.
stories.picture: A folding scale held up against a grey lake: in one pan three Frankish pennies with a king's monogram, in the other half a dirham and a nugget of amber; a broad Dane's hand holding the beam, a Frisian's face behind it, doubtful.

beats.text: Sigimar the moneyer takes old coin and foreign silver at a loss he names himself, and says a penny is worth what the king says.
Ketil weighs your pennies as silver and nothing more. The new heavy ones do well. The old light ones he hands back with one finger. This is the first place your purse is worth less than its count.

He shows you three silvers on his palm: a penny, half a dirham with writing like worm tracks, and a thick old coin with a crowned head no one can name. He nicks each with his knife. All three are good. Only one, he says, has to be explained to anybody.

The goldsmith will sell you a folding scale and eight weights, and will not sell you the knowing of them: that is three evenings at Ketil's bench, cutting and weighing until your cut pieces come out even.
Holmfast checks your Truso weights against his own, twice, and then against a third set. They agree. He is almost disappointed, and after that he deals with you as with a man who cannot be shorted.
Dragomir has a cut dirham on a thong and wants to know what the Franks would give for a bag of them. You are now one of the few men on the coast who can tell him.
You lay eastern silver on Sigimar's bench and name its weight before he does. He weighs it. He does not thank you.
A goldsmith on the Danes' river in Skane hears that Ketil's weights still agree with his, and pretends to doubt it. They came off the same mould. He tries yours against both.

The Curonian who runs the market on the hornbeam hill knows the Dane's prices and the Dane knows his: they send each other false ones by every ship. He asks you for the true one, and watches which you give.

endings.how: You sat the three evenings, bought the scale and carried eastern silver to the Rhine by weight.
endings.text: The house reckons three ways from then on: by tale in Francia, by weight in the north, by the nick everywhere. Ketil's weights go to your heir in their bronze case.
endings.reward: Sets sv_scale and sv_first_dirham; northern buyers stop shorting you; with sv_moneyer_trusts, the loss at Dorestad's mint is halved. The unlock truso.ketils_weights.

endings.how: You held to the king's penny, like Aldger, and sold here only for goods.
endings.text: You never lose a grain to a strange coin, and never gain one. Ketil says it is a respectable way to stay small.
endings.reward: No loss on silver in the east, ever; barter only at Truso (cloth for marten, iron for amber) at a fair rate; Aldger content, Ravn scornful.

endings.how: You tried to pass the old light pennies here by count, on someone who could not weigh.
endings.text: It works once, on a gatherer from the low bench. Nameda hears by evening. After that every heap you are shown on this shore has resin in it.
endings.reward: A few pennies' gain; sets tr_short_weight: prices on the beach worse until you make it good with a gift of cloth.

stories.reward: The northern reckoning: a scale, the weights, the nick test, and a host who trusts your silver without looking twice.

stories.title: Amber for the count's lady
stories.summary: A house that owes the Wōkerer of Dorestad may be given an errand in place of part of the silver: amber for his wife, matched and clear, from the shore where it is gathered and not through three hands. At the lake of the Este the gleaner's widow sorts it from the bowl and not from the heap, and the price is silver, or cloth, or a risk.
stories.picture: A cloth spread on a boat shore: a small weathered woman holding a wooden bowl of clear honey-coloured beads up to a southern merchant, a heap of rough amber by her knee, strings of beads turning in the wind at the doors of small houses behind.

beats.text: The count's steward names the errand that will stand for part of what your house owes: amber for the count's lady, a string to wear to Mass, matched and clear. It is to come from the far shore where it is gathered. He hangs a short stick on the nail beside the long one.

Nameda hears that it is for a great man's wife and puts the heap aside. From a bowl she picks beads that swim in brine and are warm on the lip, each like the next, and the cutter on the row drills them. Sixty pennies' weight, or two bolts of cloth; or a sack of raw stone, cheaper, for a house that will let the count find his own cutter.
Ketil weighs the string and keeps his mouth shut about it, which is the whole of his bargain with her. He says only that a count's wife on the Rhine will not put it in brine to see.

The steward holds out his hand. The count's lady has asked three times whether the Frisian is home. What you lay in it is held to the light of the door, and the short stick comes off the nail or stays.

endings.how: You bought the matched string for silver or for cloth and laid it in the steward's hand.
endings.text: He holds it to the light and for once says nothing about what you owe. The short stick is broken across his knee. The long one stays on its nail. She will wear the string to Mass at Easter, and the abbess will count the beads.
endings.reward: The count's errand done (db_service cleared); the toll at Dorestad eased for a season; the steward's good will. The debt itself is not lessened by any card yet.

endings.how: You bought a sack of raw stone and set it on his table as it was.
endings.text: He weighs the sack in his hand and sends a boy for the comb-maker, who cuts bone and may cut this. An errand done, he says, if not done handsomely. The lady will have to wait, and the count dislikes it when she waits.
endings.reward: The errand done more cheaply (db_service cleared); the toll eased for a month; a cooler thanks.

endings.how: You said the stone was promised elsewhere, or never brought it.
endings.text: He looks at the short stick on the nail, and then at you. It can hang there, he says. Sticks keep. So do counts' ladies, but not as well.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but the steward's patience; the errand stays open while the count lives (to 812).

stories.reward: The spine's one errand for the count from the eastern sea, the thread counts_day: amber for his wife, bought where it is gathered, and what the count's house thinks of yours afterwards.

stories.title: Eleven and five
stories.summary: In Ketil's last summers a Gute lodges at the long house, counts out eleven coins and five pieces, puts them under a floor post and goes up the Vistula with a boat of swords. He does not come back. The purse outlasts the house, the town and the game.
stories.picture: By rushlight, a man kneeling at the foot of a house post, lowering a small leather purse into a hole; on the floor beside him ten thin silver coins and one thick one with a crowned head; an old Dane holding the light and looking away.

beats.text: A Gute skipper asks Ketil for a witness from outside the shore, and Ketil points at you. Eleven whole, five cut; you count them with him. One is thick and old, with a king's head. He says a Svea gave it him for luck and it has not yet done anything.
On Gotland his wife asks whether anyone at the lake has seen him. Men there put silver under the floor and say nothing; she knows there is a floor somewhere with his in it.
A dealer who pays in dirhams and wants swords remembers a Gute with a boatload of blades, two summers back, on the southern rivers. He remembers the blades better than the man.
Asfrid knows which post. Her house does not dig under a guest's post, she says; but your house was the witness, and a witness may say whose it is now.

endings.how: You said it was his, and that he might yet send a son for it.
endings.text: It stays under the post. The house falls, the town burns, the reeds come. Eleven hundred and seventy years later someone with a trowel counts eleven and five.
endings.reward: Asfrid's whole trust: lodging and store free here for your house for good (lodge, store); a line in the house book. This is what happened.

endings.how: You dug it with Asfrid as witness and carried it to Gotland.
endings.text: The widow, or by then her son, weighs it, finds it exact, and gives you the thick old coin back: it brought his father no luck and may suit a Frisian better.
endings.reward: The Persian drachm as an heirloom (a curiosity a moneyer or an abbot will pay well to see); a friend at Paviken; sets tr_purse_home.

endings.how: You dug it and kept it.
endings.text: About forty pennies' weight of silver. Asfrid says nothing. The next time you ask for your sea chest out of her store she has trouble finding it.
endings.reward: Silver worth about 40 d; lodging and store at Truso lost; sets tr_purse_taken.

stories.reward: A place in a house's memory across three generations, or a coin of a king dead two hundred years.

stories.title: Told in order
stories.summary: About 890 an Englishman from the Heaths sits in the long house asking about the dead. Your house has been coming here for a hundred years and can tell him what its fathers saw; what he hears he will tell a king in the west, and a clerk will write it into a book.
stories.picture: The long house at evening: an Englishman of forty with a string of rough amber on his wrist counting on his fingers; across the hearth a Frisian skipper talking; a Danish woman with oval brooches drilling a bead and listening to both.

beats.text: An Englishman is fitting out for the east and asking who has made the passage. Seven days and nights, somebody says. He wants to know what lies to port.
Wulfstan at the hearth. He has seen the mares' milk and the mead. He has been told about the cold and the heaps and wants someone who was there, or whose grandfather was.
A rich man is to burn tomorrow. You can take the Englishman up to the palings with you, if the fort still seats your house; otherwise he stands on the beach and hears the hooves.
A priest who copies books for the king has a quire about the north. One passage begins: Wulfstan said that he went from the Heaths. You know the rest before he reads it.

At the river mouth in Skane a woman selling from a chest lid remembers the Englishman: he put in for water and asked the name of every headland in sight. She answered them all, she says, and sold him nothing.

endings.how: You told him what your house saw and no more, and took him to the palings.
endings.text: He tells it to the king in order: the kings, the drink, the month in the house, the heaps, the horses, the cold. It is the only account of this shore that will ever be written.
endings.reward: give_text wulfstan, free, at Hamwic, Lundenwic or Eoforwic; the copying priest's goodwill; Wulfstan a friend at the Heaths. This is what happened.

endings.how: You improved on it: bigger heaps, colder cold, a king dead a full year.
endings.text: He listens, thanks you, and keeps only what Asfrid tells him afterwards. Half a year, he says in the end; and 'sometimes'.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but his good opinion; a dry line from Asfrid. The book is the same.

endings.how: You said a house's knowledge is its stock, and sold him amber instead.
endings.text: He learns it anyway, more slowly. He buys your amber at a fair price and does not ask you anything again.
endings.reward: A good sale of amber for the English market; no text; no friend.

stories.reward: The game's own source, handed back: the voyage of Wulfstan for the chest, and a friend who sails the same road.

stories.title: The reeds
stories.summary: In the last fifty years the channel closes a hand's breadth each spring and the ships go to the new harbour at the Vistula's mouth. Then one night there are arrows and fire. What a house with a century of friends here does about it is small, and is all there is.
stories.picture: A narrow lane of brown water between walls of reed, a ship being hauled through it on a rope by men on the bank, a fisherman in her bow with a tall sounding pole; behind, thatched roofs and a new earth bank.

beats.text: In the Dane's day the river mouth is open water, and a man named Santirme brings ships up to the houses under sail, for salt. He says the reeds stand a little further out each spring, and that nobody but his kin is counting.
Mante takes the pole. Your grandfather came up to the houses under oars, he says; you will go in on a rope. A hand less water than at the last thaw.
Half the plots have no smoke. Asfrid's great-grandchildren are selling the long house for what its timber is worth and asking what a plot costs at the Vistula's mouth.

News a season old: a shaved man with a book went among the forts after the thaw and was killed, and a duke bought him back for his weight in gold. Mante thinks the duke will want more than a body for that gold.
Charred posts above the reeds. Mante, or his son, tells you which night, and that he counted boats and not faces.

The Gotlanders at the new quays say nobody goes to the lake of the Este now. There is a harbour with a wall at the Vistula's mouth, a day nearer the sea. One old man remembers a long house there, and a woman who drilled beads.

endings.how: Before the fire you carried the long house's people and stock down to the Vistula's mouth in your own ship, for nothing.
endings.text: They set up a bench and a scale in the new harbour. The first weights they put on it are an old Dane's, in a round bronze case.
endings.reward: A friend's house, lodging and store at the new harbour for your heirs (for whoever writes that port); the best of the last amber at the old price.

endings.how: You paid for the channel to be staked and cleared, year after year.
endings.text: It holds a little longer than it would have. Ships that would have turned back at the Ilfing come up to the houses for another ten springs. Then the river wins.
endings.reward: Truso stays open to a sea-going ship while the work truso.work.channel is kept up (to 1000); Mante pilots you free for life.

endings.how: You came, traded and left, like everyone else, until there was nothing to come to.
endings.text: One spring you find ash. Mante sells you a sack of amber on the shore where the weighing ground was, and weighs it on a scale with a burnt case.
endings.reward: Nothing but the knowing; a line for the house book: 'This year Truso was not there.'

stories.reward: An ending kept in the family: the people of the long house carried to the next harbour, or a channel that bears your stakes.

works.name: A house on a marked plot
works.what: A small post-built house and a fenced plot in the row along the shore, between a comb-maker and a Gute: a bench, a hearth, a locked chest and room to draw the boat up before the door.
works.needs: The fort's leave: a seat in the fort that is not by the door (chain amber_road, or three gifts to Gedune or his heirs), and Ketil's house to speak for you. Not if ch_amber_road_truso_shut.
works.gives: Lodging and store of your own here (lodge, store); goods may be left over winter and sold by a factor at the spring price; sets unlock_plot_truso.
works.picture: Two men setting split-oak posts in a row of holes on a fenced strip of shore, a small boat drawn up at its foot, thatch bundles stacked ready.
works.source: Houses in regularly marked-out plots; small houses of about 5 by 10 m (pl. and en.wikipedia 'Truso'). How a stranger got a plot is not known (?)

works.name: Stakes in the channel
works.what: Alder stakes with withy tops driven along both sides of the way through the reeds, from the Ilfing's mouth to the boat shore, and the weed cut between them. The fishers do it; someone has to pay the fishers.
works.needs: A fisher of the Ilfing who knows this spring's channel (Mante after 950; his fathers before). Must be done again every third spring, and every spring after 960.
works.gives: No pilot needed and no risk of grounding between the lagoon and the shore; after 950 it keeps the port open to a sea-going ship for as long as it is kept up.
works.picture: A fisherman standing in a log boat driving a stake with a wooden maul, a line of stakes with bushy tops leading away through reeds to open water.
works.source: Lake Druzno shallow and reed-ringed (en.wikipedia 'Lake Druzno'); the silting of the later 10th century (en.wikipedia 'Truso'). Staked channels are ordinary practice on shallow waters; none is recorded here (?)

works.name: A cold pit under your floor
works.what: A pit dug under the bench of your house, lined with moss and straw and packed at midwinter with lake ice by Drua's kin. That is half of what they do. The other half they keep.
works.needs: A house on a plot here; and to have asked how the cold is made and been shown (flag ch_amber_road_cold_known), or a standing gift to Drua's kin each midwinter.
works.gives: Fish, butter and meat keep through summer in your store here; a guest who dies under your roof can wait for his kin. Leads to the ice chest for the ship (unlock_upgrade_ice_chest).
works.picture: A lifted floor board in a dark house showing a pit packed with grey ice and straw, an old woman's hand resting on the board's edge.
works.source: Wulfstan on the kin who can make cold (Old English Orosius). An ice pit is the modern guess and is what the chain shows as 'half' (?)

works.name: A brewhouse inside the palings
works.what: A log house with a mash tub, a kettle and a brew-wife from the west, inside the fort, making a drink that is neither the king's milk nor the slave's mead.
works.needs: The ale ending of the chain amber_road (flag ch_amber_road_end_ale); malt carried from the west.
works.gives: Malt and barley wanted at Truso at double for a year and steadily after; the king's hand on your boat; sets unlock_work_truso_brewhouse. This changes what Wulfstan is told in 890.
works.picture: Inside a palisade, a strong woman with rolled sleeves stirring a steaming tub with a paddle while horsemen with milk bowls stand watching in a half circle.
works.source: Against the record on purpose: 'no ale is brewed among the Este, but there is mead enough' (Wulfstan). The chain's changed-history ending (Design/content/chains/amber_road.md)

works.name: A share in the bank and ditch
works.what: Two months of men and timber toward a ditch and an earth bank round the landward side of the plots, which the town has never had.
works.needs: A house on a plot here; the fort's king and the shore's householders agreed, which takes a feast.
works.gives: Your store here is safe from a raid by land; every householder's feeling toward you warmer; when the fire comes, your people have a night's warning and get to the boats.
works.picture: Men with wooden spades and baskets throwing up a raw earth bank beside a new ditch, thatched houses close behind them, a boy carrying a sheaf of arrows.
works.source: Defences raised about 950 (sv.wikipedia 'Truso' (?)); a boundary ditch reported by the excavator (?); the ash layer with arrowheads (en.wikipedia 'Truso')

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The boat of this shore: riveted in the Scandinavian way, nine to eleven metres, broad and shallow enough for the lake and the Estmere. The menders build one at a time when a buyer leaves silver in autumn.
ships.picture: A broad shallow clinker boat on blocks on a reedy shore, lines of iron rivets along her strakes, a tar barrel and a hurdle of drying moss beside her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json (riveted boats at Truso and Grobina); Design/content/ships.md, boats of 9 to 11 m by 2.5 to 3 m from an abstract (?); rivets and wreckage (pl.wikipedia 'Truso')

ships.note: A four-oar or six-oar boat off the shore, sold when its owner burns: his kin would rather have silver for the drinking than a boat.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat lying on grey shingle with her oars pushed under the thwarts, a woman with a rake walking past her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json. That a dead man's goods are drunk and ridden away (Wulfstan) is why such a boat comes up for sale: the game's reading

ships.note: The fishers of the Ilfing stand in hollowed trunks. One goes where no keel goes: up the creeks, through the reeds, and after 1000 it is the only boat that reaches the old shore at all.
ships.picture: A dark hollowed log with a fisherman standing in it, poling between walls of reed in early light.
ships.source: The game's for this place (?): logboats are the common small craft of the Baltic lakes and rivers (ship_classes_793.json)

ships.note: A Gute's or a Svea's ship, sold on the shore by a man going inland up the Vistula in something smaller, or by his heirs when he does not come back. Not built here: there is no slip long enough.
ships.picture: A lean riveted ship of a dozen oars a side drawn half out of brown lake water, her mast lowered, a man in an eastern-cut coat counting silver on her gunwale.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json; the road north to Birka by Gotland and inland by the Vistula (en.wikipedia 'Truso'; Medievalists.net 2026). No such sale is recorded (?)

sayings.text: The king and the richest men drink mares' milk, and the poor and the slaves drink mead.
sayings.source: Wulfstan, in the Old English Orosius (Sweet 1883, p. 20); our rendering from the Old English

sayings.text: There is no ale brewed among the Este, but there is mead enough.
sayings.source: Wulfstan, in the Old English Orosius (Sweet 1883, p. 20); our rendering

sayings.text: In every fort there is a king.
sayings.source: Wulfstan, in the Old English Orosius (Sweet 1883, p. 20); our rendering

sayings.text: A dead man here is the best host in the country: he pays for the drink a month and takes no offence.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Wulfstan's account of the wake

sayings.text: A slow horse eats as much as a fast one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the Este's reason for the price of horses, Wulfstan)
invented in the period's manner; the scales and weights of the dig

sayings.text: A king far off once wrote to tell us what amber is. We were glad to know. We had only been picking it up.
sayings.source: a dry turn on Theodoric's letter to the Aesti (Cassiodorus, Variae V.2); that it was remembered here is the game's (?)

sayings.text: A wonder was on the way: water was turned to bone.
sayings.source: Exeter Book riddle 68-69 (texts_793.json exeter_68_69_ice), our rendering of the last line: the answer is ice. Wigmar's father's riddle (chain amber_road)
Hávamál 41 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_041): said by the Danes of the shore

sayings.text: The Frisian thinks the sea-stone cheap, the Este thinks the cloak cheap, and both go home laughing. It is the only honest trade.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Adam of Bremen IV.18 (marten skins for woollen cloaks; later)

easter_eggs.text: On Ketil's palm, among the thin coins with worm-track writing, one is thicker, with a crowned head and a fire altar: a king of the Persians dead two hundred years, still passing as silver. In the purse under the post it is the eleventh.
easter_eggs.source: The drachm of Khosrow II (died 628) in the deposit dug at Truso in 1986 (Medievalists.net 2026)

easter_eggs.text: Rub a piece of true amber hard on a wool sleeve and hold it over the chips on the cutter's floor: they jump to it. Nameda calls this 'the stone being hungry'.
easter_eggs.source: True of amber (the Greeks' elektron); the test is the chain's. Her phrase is invented

easter_eggs.text: The fishers at the river mouth say the name of the place means the reeds. The Danes say it means 'hurry up'. Neither will give way.
easter_eggs.source: The two unsettled etymologies of Truso (de.wikipedia 'Truso'); called the oldest place-name recorded on the Baltic shore (Gimbutas, in en.wikipedia 'Truso')

easter_eggs.text: A gatherer on the low bench uses a word for amber that sounds like 'glass'. Eight hundred years before, a Roman wrote that the people of this shore call it glesum, gather it in the shallows, and are astonished to be paid.
easter_eggs.source: Tacitus, Germania 45 (about AD 98), of the Aestii. That the word was still used in 793 is the game's (?)

easter_eggs.text: In the woods a morning's walk north, a man who did not trust houses put six coins and two pieces under a root.
easter_eggs.source: The dirhams found near Mlynary, north of Elblag, reported in autumn 2026 (Medievalists.net)

easter_eggs.text: At a burning, count the heaps: five, or six. Then count the riders who go home with nothing. The dead man's children are among them.
easter_eggs.source: Wulfstan: the estate is drunk and ridden away by strangers, and that is why nothing is left (Old English Orosius)

easter_eggs.text: After 1000, a fisherman shows you where the town was by pointing with his pole at a place in the reeds that looks like every other place in the reeds. Men will look for it in the wrong village for sixty years before they find it.
easter_eggs.source: Placed at Hansdorf from finds of 1897 and digs of the 1920s; found for certain at Janow Pomorski by Marek F. Jagodzinski from 1981 (en. and de.wikipedia 'Truso')

unlocks.what: Ketil's scale and eight weights, in a round bronze case
unlocks.how: Sit three evenings at his bench cutting and weighing silver (story truso.kings_head), and buy the scale from the goldsmith.
unlocks.gives: flag sv_scale; weigh_silver and test_silver anywhere without a fee; no short weight from northern buyers. Passes to your heir.

unlocks.what: Nameda's three tests for amber: the sleeve, the brine, the lip
unlocks.how: Buy nothing from her and ask to be shown (chain amber_road s04), or be cheated once and go back.
unlocks.gives: learn: no false amber in any sack you buy, at Truso or anywhere; the amber-cutters at Ripa and Sliesthorp pay your price without sorting.

unlocks.what: The way in: the gap in the spit, the Estmere, the Ilfing, the lake
unlocks.how: Make the passage three times with a fisher of the Ilfing in the bow, or take it as the chain's reward (unlock_pilot_estmere).
unlocks.gives: No pilot needed from the sea to the shore; a day saved on every call; the chest text wulfstan reads as a pilot's rutter to you.

unlocks.what: A seat in the fort among the men who own horses
unlocks.how: Take the mares' milk and drink all of it; give the fort's king a gift on two calls; never be found with a bone unburnt.
unlocks.gives: audience and feast at the fort; the king's store sells to you before the beach; horses may be bought on the mile road. Lost with ch_amber_road_truso_shut.

unlocks.what: Your house's name in the long house
unlocks.how: Lodge with Ketil on three calls, or stand witness to the purse (story truso.eleven_and_five).
unlocks.gives: lodge and store free here; Asfrid and her children greet your heirs by the house's name, to the end of the town; prices and news of the last ship told without asking.

unlocks.how: Pay for the channel stakes (truso.work.channel) or buy their catch on every call.
unlocks.gives: ask_harbour here tells who has come and gone since the thaw, by people and by cargo; a warning if armed boats are in the Estmere.
